summary:
Navan's architecture team, Roberto Milev and Uday Kanagala, presents a production-tested reference architecture for agentic AI, framing agents as analogous to where microservices stood around 2015. They invoke the maxim that a poorly structured monolith should precede any move to microservices, and translate this to agents: one should not reach for a multi-agent orchestrated system before mastering a single agentic loop. They close by assessing where the field is mature and where it is still open.

The architecture is described as layered. At the runtime layer, agents are stateful, requiring persistent sessions, isolation, and lifecycle handling; Navan runs on AWS AgentCore with custom session persistence and rehydration. The memory layer has evolved from simple RAG into ingestion, extraction, consolidation, and retrieval, covering short-term, long-term, and episodic memory. Context management centers on skills as the unit of context — instructions paired with tool execution — composed dynamically via progressive disclosure. Uday adds operational layers: pre- and post-tool-call hooks plus auto traces that emit goal, reasoning, belief status, and a confidence score, with inferred answers routed to humans; testing via trajectory scoring rather than output assertion; and guardrails before and after every tool call to handle the blurred user-versus-agent authorization line. Navan prefers a single master agent that progressively loads skills.

In the closing stack assessment, runtime, orchestration, memory, MCP-based tool calling, and testing patterns are framed as mostly solved or converging, while observability (OTEL for agentic calls), cost prediction and management, replay and debugging, and standards (A2A, OTEL) remain genuinely open. The talk ends with a call that the community now knows what to build.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: If you cannot build a well-structured monolith, do not reach for microservices — and if you cannot build a single agentic loop, do not reach for multi-agent orchestration.

Agents are stateful by nature, requiring persistent sessions, isolation, and lifecycle handling that AWS AgentCore only partially covers, so Navan built session persistence and rehydration themselves.
Skills — pairs of contextual instructions plus tool execution — are Navan's chosen unit of context, composed dynamically via progressive disclosure.
Traditional logs fail for agents because of the volume of reasoning; pre- and post-tool-call hooks plus auto traces with goal, reasoning, belief, and confidence signals replace them.
Testing shifts from asserting outputs to scoring trajectories — how far the agent progressed from source toward goal.
Guardrails run before and after every tool call, enabling fine-grained authorization where agents may act on behalf of users or under their own service accounts.
MCP has emerged as the de facto tool-calling protocol and is evolving toward statelessness, signaling industry convergence.
Runtime, orchestration, memory, MCP, and testing patterns are largely solved or converging, while cost, replay/debugging, OTEL for agentic calls, and standards (A2A) remain open problems.
Map the emerging reference architecture layers — runtime, memory, context, observability, guardrails, orchestration — for production agentic systems.
Apply progressive skill loading as a strategy for managing context windows.

sections.title: Microservices analogy and paradigm shifts
sections.summary: Roberto opens by noting paradigm shifts like the microservices bandwagon, quoting the principle that you should not build microservices unless you can build a well-structured monolith. He translates this to agents: if you cannot build a single agentic loop, do not attempt multi-agent orchestration. He introduces an emerging reference architecture with layers for runtime, memory, context, operations, and orchestration.

sections.title: Runtime and memory layers
sections.summary: Roberto describes agents as stateful, needing persistent sessions, isolation, and lifecycles unlike stateless APIs. He surveys AWS, GCP, and Azure agentic runtimes and explains that Navan runs on AWS AgentCore, filling gaps in session persistence and rehydration. He then walks through memory evolution from RAG to an ingestion-extraction-consolidation-retrieval pipeline, covering short-term, long-term, and episodic memory.

sections.title: Context management via skills
sections.summary: Roberto introduces skills as the unit of context, pairing instructions with tool execution. Context is composed dynamically from pluggable, independently testable, reusable skills, using progressive disclosure to start narrow and expand with metadata over time. He hands off to Uday for the operational layers.

sections.title: Observability with hooks and traces
sections.summary: Uday argues traditional logs fail when agents emit extensive thinking. Using Claude's hooks as an example, he explains intercepting pre- and post-tool-call and pre/post-decision points to emit auto traces capturing the current goal, reasoning, belief status, tool calls, and a confidence score. Inferred answers are flagged for human-in-the-loop review.

sections.title: Trajectory-based testing
sections.summary: Uday addresses the difficulty of testing non-deterministic agents. Because you cannot chart a deterministic graph, Navan relies on trajectory evaluation — measuring how far the agent progressed from source to goal — and uses inferred-answer signals to detect regressions. Changing one component often breaks another, making this scoring approach essential.

sections.title: Guardrails and authorization
sections.summary: Uday describes guardrails as critical for enterprise AI because sensitive data flows into models. Traditional user-vs-service-account authorization blurs when an agent acts on behalf of a user — for example, autonomously booking a flight when fares drop below $200 — or under its own service account. Navan runs guardrails before and after every tool call to make fine-grained authorization decisions.

sections.title: Single master agent versus multi-agent
sections.summary: Reinforcing Roberto's monolith caution, Uday states Navan prefers a single master agent that progressively loads skills and may invoke sub-agents. He acknowledges other emerging patterns, including A2A as a protocol that establishes skill contracts across team boundaries.

sections.title: Stack maturity and open problems
sections.summary: Roberto surveys the stack: runtime, orchestration, memory, and MCP-based tool calling are largely solved or converging, while testing patterns are getting better defined. Observability via OTEL works with effort, cost prediction and management remain hard, replay and debugging are open but may be solved with agent-assisted debugging, and A2A plus OTEL are emerging standards. He closes that the community knows what to build.

limitations: Cost remains genuinely unsolved: hard to predict, manage, and put guardrails around.
Replay and debugging of agent behavior are still hard, though agents may eventually help.
OTEL was not designed for agentic calls and only works with effort.
A2A is young and driven by certain vendors, not yet a settled standard.
Logs stop working because agents emit too much thinking.
Trajectory scoring cannot chart a fully deterministic graph because agents are non-deterministic.
Old user-versus-service-principal authorization model does not survive contact with agents acting on behalf of users or under their own service accounts.
quantitativeClaims: Agents execute multi-step processes spanning roughly 20 to 30 steps where traditional logs become unreadable.
Navan consumes a high volume of tokens per day across many agents in production.
